messages.subject_clean: Snapshots and point transect DS
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I've some experience in line transect DS, and DS using camera-traps following Howe et al 2019 (https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.12790); but I'm new in point-transect DS.

My concern:

I’m now working on a project to estimate the Iberian goat (mountain ungulate) population density. This species is usually monitored from points and applying total counts or point-transect DS. However, I think that considering the theoretical background of CTDS will be very useful for this species, but considering human observers instead of camera-traps. So, the question is, do you think that it is correct to define snapshots moments considering a point-transect DS based on human observers? (obviously, during the analysis, I'll consider overdispersion: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13082).

Considering the habitat selected by these animals, the human effort of traveling between sampling points is very high. So in my opinion, it could be cost-efficient if we can carry out more than one sampling during each visit by considering snapshot moments (let say, 30min apart to locate and identify objects around the point).

 THANK YOU VERY MUCH!

Best

Pablo

messages.subject: Model design for post stratification in r
messages.subject_clean: Model design for post stratification in r
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

  Hoping to get some advice regarding model design in r, using the 'Distance' package. This is basic stuff, but I am finding it hard to find advise/ help/ working examples for the r package as opposed to the Distance software. I have one site, fairly small in size (approximately 222.5 ha) which I have been surveying once every few months. I am doing point surveys, from the same points each time and currently have 10 surveys spanning over 2 years. Due to ongoing construction work at the site, the number of times each point was visited was not consistent for all points and 'Effort' is set as the number of times each point was visited. I have 209 observations to clusters of animals (1-6 in size).

The number of animals recorded at different times of the year has important management implications for the site and therefore I am interested in the population density for each survey, as well as an overall population estimate. This is where I am getting a little confused. As populations for this species fluctuate, the number recorded at each survey are different and I have therefore included the survey number (Survey_Number) as a covariate into my ds() model, as below:

covar.model<- ds(point_cuts, transect = "point", key="hn",adjustment = NULL,
                                formula=~as.factor(Survey_Number),
                                convert.units = unit_conversion_point)

I then use this model in a dht2 model to stratify by the survey number (1-10) and to tell the model that they are replicates.  I have set stratification to 'effort_sum' due to the low number of replicates (10). I have set sample_fraction=0.5 as only 180 degrees of the point is visible (I am aware this is usually used for line transects).

Model <- dht2(model.hn <http://model.hn>, flatfile=point_cuts, strat_formula = ~Survey_Number,
                                 stratification = "effort_sum",sample_fraction = 0.5, total_area = 222.5,
                                 ci_width = 0.95, convert_units = unit_conversion_point)

My question is whether I am reasonably on the right track and if this method is appropriate? This model (below) gives a reasonable estimate of the population size, but the output estimates the surveyed area area as being higher than available area for some surveys. Is this likely to be an error with effort?

I would greatly appreciate any help or advise as I have been going around in circles for this for quite a long time!

Thanks,
Sam

messages.body_plain:
Sam

Thanks for the note; there's quite a lot to unpack.  My comments are in no particular order
inclusion of Survey_Number as a covariate in your detection function model won't necessarily account for fluctuations in abundance with time.  Rather, the use of a covariate implies that detectability of the target species changes with time.
the explanation for CoveredArea exceeding study area size is that the calculation of CoveredArea includes the repeat visits to points, not an error--merely the way CoveredArea is calculated.
from the summary it seems not only are the number of visits variable throughout the study (Effort), but the number of points visited (k) vary throughout the study; is that correct?
the most telling aspects of the output you provided is the variability in encounter rate for the different surveys.  The number of replicate point stations (not number of visits) is pretty small--falling as low as 4 or 5.  That implies that the variability in encounter rate between points cannot be estimated very well (note the size of the encounter rate CV for surveys 7 and 8 when number of stations is small: >100%).  This encounter rate variability propagates into the uncertainty in the survey-specific densities; they all have CVs of 0.3 or larger.  I'm not sure I would put much confidence in those survey-specific estimates.
there does seem to be something not quite right with the confidence interval calculations; several of which range from 0 to infinity.  As I said, those survey-specific estimates are imprecise, but perhaps not that imprecise.
would you please re-run your analysis using "replicate" as the value of the stratification argument in your call to `dht2`.  I'm curious to know whether the confidence interval values are better behaved when using that option.  We've not had much experience with the behaviour of the "effort-sum" computations.
Let me know what you find.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Eric,

 Thanks very much for your reply. Apologies in my delay of getting back to you. I took on board what you said and have been examining the data again, unfortunately, to little avail.

Thank you for the explanation regarding the surveyed sample area- I had seen in several examples that the calculated area exceeded the actual area and was not sure why this could be the case.

Yes, you are correct in saying that the number of points and the number of visits to these points varied. Unfortunately, there were construction works going on in the area which meant that not all survey points were available at all times in the Northern half of the site. However, along the Southern half of the site, the points (n=9) remained untouched and were surveyed 10 times each. However, if I run the data just of the southern half of the site, ignoring the northern half where construction work was ongoing, I run into similar issues of very large (and incorrect) confidence intervals of 0- Inf. I imagine,  this is due to the same problem of just having too few replicate point stations.

I ran the same model with 'replicate' set as the stratification argument, as suggested (output below). The same issues are still present, except that the SE and CV are now zero for the 'Total'.

I think what you are saying from your reply above is that there are not enough detections to look at density on an individual survey level. Stratifying by season may be an option, but I unfortunately have uneven sampling for seasons down to surveys being taken monthly along with Covid (!) having put a 6 month pause on fieldwork. As you can see from the output below, the confidence intervals are better fitted but the CV and CV.ER <http://CV.ER> are still too high. Is this something that is likely to  improve with further data collection?

Best wishes,
Sam

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am hoping to get some advice on how to treat multi-species feeding flocks when collecting and analysing data.

For my honours project I am carrying out a survey to estimate the abundance of winter resident birds in a woodland using distance sampling in 30 point count stations. Some of these species often occur in multi-species feeding flocks in winter and I was planning to include species as covariate in the detection function as I doubt I will collect enough data for each one.

I found out about distance sampling while researching for this project, and although I am trying to read as much as possible on this, I am not finding many information on multi species flocks. I have three issues regarding this topic:

I am not sure whether I should record my observations as clusters or individuals as it is unclear to me whether when I read about clusters, this refers to single species clusters only or multi species groups as well.
Within these flocks non-targeted species can be observed. Therefore, if my observations are treated as clusters, should the cluster size include these non-targeted species as well?
Some of the targeted species also occur individually and it is unclear to me whether I can combine the two data sets (clusters and non) to calculate abundance.
I hope I gave enough information to understand my problem,
Thank you so much!

Eleonora

messages.body_plain:
Eleonora

Welcome to the world of distance sampling, I hope you find it interesting.  For the most part, discussion of animals occurring in groups in distance sampling refers to single species groups.  The occurrence of mixed-species groups is problematic.

There are published approaches (and software) for dealing with the mixed groups, but this adds a considerable level of complexity to the analysis.  For completeness, here are references to a paper describing mixed-species groups (of dolphins) and a link to the R package (mads) for dealing with mixed groups.
Gerrodette, T., & Forcada, J. (2005). Non-recovery of two spotted and spinner dolphin populations in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. Marine Ecology Progress Series, 291, 1–21. https://doi.org/10.3354/meps291001
Marshall, L. (2020). mads: Multi-Analysis Distance Sampling (0.1.6) [Computer software]. https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=mads
As an approximate approach to estimating abundance for your project, perhaps the simple path is to treat all of your detections as detections of individuals.  For example if there is a flock of 20 birds, the centre of which is at 30m from the point count station, record 15 detections of SpA and 5 detections of SpB, all at distance 30m.  This way, you can omit the non-target species from the recording.  That should also resolve your third question.  Rational for treating detection of a group as detection of multiple individuals is discussed in this reference:
Buckland, S. T., Plumptre, A. J., Thomas, L., & Rexstad, E. A. (2010). Design and analysis of line transect surveys for primates. International Journal of Primatology, 31, 833–847. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10764-010-9431-5

Training workshop on distance sampling when animals are missed at zero
distance

Registration is now open for our latest online interactive training
workshop.  Join us by video from anywhere around the world!  For full
details, and to register, please go to

http://workshops.distancesampling.org/mrds-jan-2021.html

Workshop Overview

Conventional distance sampling methods assume that all animals at zero
distance are detected with certainty.  However, in some situations this
assumption is violated, and some animals are missed, causing a negative
bias in the density and abundance estimates.

This occurs on some shipboard surveys of marine mammals, for example,
where animals may be missed on the trackline because they are underwater
while the survey vessel passes, or because the sea conditions are rough
so that even some animals right on the line are missed.  The former
(being underwater and so not available for detection) is often called
availability bias and the latter perception bias.

In this two-day workshop, we cover survey protocols and analytical
methods for dealing with both perception bias and availability bias.
The workshop is intended for those already familiar with the basics of
distance sampling.

Instructors

messages.body_plain:
Cheryl, yes, in those days, typically people didn’t record groups.  You should be able to analyse the data ignoring this issue, but I would suggest carrying out 2 checks:  1. Select the bootstrap for variance estimation resampling points, and see if this makes much difference to variance estimates and confidence intervals.  (The bootstrap assumes independent points but individual detections at a single point are not assumed to be independent.  But the analytic estimates are pretty robust to non-independence, so this shouldn’t make much difference.  And 2. Try reanalysing the data by putting observations at the same time, location and distance into a group, and re-analyse the grouped data.  Again, you should get very similar results given the robustness of the methods, but this is worth checking.

No problem at all that you get multiple birds at a single location – perturbing distances a little has no advantages, and will add a little noise.  If however there is a lot of rounding in the data, you should consider grouping the distances before analysis, with group cutpoints avoiding favoured rounding distances.

Steve Buckland
